podcast.title: Death (June 2022)
podcast.body: Dave Bartholomew, the long-time collaborator and producer for Fats Domino, passed away in June of the current year (relative to the podcast's original broadcast), at the remarkable age of 100. He left behind one of the finest legacies in the histories of rock and roll, rhythm and blues, and New Orleans music. "His collaborator Dave Bartholomew died in June this year, aged 100."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: "Country Boy" - Pioneering Horn Part
podcast.body: "Country Boy" featured a distinct "Dan. Da da" horn part that, while clichéd today, was unprecedented in an R&B record at its time of release. "that was the first time anything like that had been used in an A&B record."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 8: The Fat Man and Fats Domino

podcast.title: "Juncker's Blues" Lyrics - Unsuitable for Radio
podcast.body: Dave Bartholomew initially wanted Fats Domino to record "Juncker's Blues," but its original lyrics, largely about heroin and cocaine, were deemed inappropriate for radio airplay. "it was felt that the lyrics weren't quite suitable for the radio, what would them be pretty much entirely about heroin and cocaine."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 8: The Fat Man and Fats Domino

podcast.title: "The Fat Man" Lyrics - Blues Trope of Body Positivity and Attraction
podcast.body: Dave Bartholomew's lyrics for "The Fat Man" employ a common blues trope where a large man boasts about his attractiveness to women despite his size. "follow a standard blues trope of being fat but having the ability to attract women anyway."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 8: The Fat Man and Fats Domino

podcast.title: Attempt to Block "Blueberry Hill"
podcast.body: Initially unenthusiastic about recording "Blueberry Hill," Dave Bartholomew famously declared "we got nothing" at the end of the session and later tried to prevent its release, telling Imperial Records owner Lou Chudd that it would "ruin Domino's career forever." He later admitted this was a "huge mistake," recognizing the song's massive success and stating that his arrangement for it would be his lasting legacy. "When I'm dead and gone a million times, they'll still be playing, that the dad the dad did that."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Composer of "My Ding-a-Ling"
podcast.body: Dave Bartholomew wrote "My Ding-a-Ling," the novelty song that became Chuck Berry's only number one hit in the 1970s. "his only number one, with a novelty song by Dave Bartholomew, My Dingling."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Dave Bartholomew's Formal Musical Training - Military Brass Band
podcast.body: His time in a military brass band necessitated Dave Bartholomew's acquisition of more formal musical skills, including composition and arrangement. "once he was put into a military brass band, he had to learn more formal musical skills, including writing and arranging."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 8: The Fat Man and Fats Domino

podcast.title: Dave Bartholomew's Military Service and Musical Development
podcast.body: Like many New Orleans musicians of the late 1940s, Dave Bartholomew honed and expanded his musical abilities during his service in the Army during World War II. "Dave Bartholomew learned his musical skills while he was in the Army during World War II."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 8: The Fat Man and Fats Domino

podcast.title: Dave Bartholomew's Post-Army Career - A&R and Orchestra Leader
podcast.body: After his military service, Dave Bartholomew secured an A&R position with Imperial Records and established the Dave Bartholomew Orchestra, which achieved a hit with the song "Country Boy." "After getting out of the Army, he got work as an A&R man for Imperial Records, and he also formed his own band, the Dave Bartholomew Orchestra, who had a hit with Country Boy."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 8: The Fat Man and Fats Domino

podcast.title: Dave Bartholomew's Rhythmic Innovation - Habanera vs. Backbeat
podcast.body: Dave Bartholomew pioneered the practice of placing the Habanera rhythm against a drum shuffle or backbeat, an innovation that gave New Orleans R&B its unique flavor. "That rhythm was put against drums playing a shuffle or a backbeat."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 8: The Fat Man and Fats Domino

podcast.title: Dave Bartholomew's Role in Fats Domino's Signing
podcast.body: Dave Bartholomew, the leading New Orleans musician of his time and an A&R man for Imperial Records, was instrumental in suggesting the label sign Fats Domino, recognizing his talent. "Bartholomew, who was working for Imperial Records, suggested that the label signed Domino."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 8: The Fat Man and Fats Domino

podcast.title: Dave Bartholomew's Session Musicians - Consistent Lineup
podcast.body: The musicians who played on "Country Boy" became Dave Bartholomew's core session band, consistently employed for numerous productions over many years. "The musicians on Country Boy, were ones that Bartholomew would continue to employ for many years on all the sessions he produced."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 8: The Fat Man and Fats Domino

podcast.title: Dave Bartholomew's Trumpet Training - Louis Armstrong Connection
podcast.body: Dave Bartholomew was already a proficient trumpet player, having received instruction from the same teacher who also taught the legendary Louis Armstrong. "having been taught by the same man who taught Louis Armstrong."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 8: The Fat Man and Fats Domino

podcast.title: Habanera-Backbeat Combination - Dave Bartholomew's Innovation
podcast.body: Dave Bartholomew and his musicians are credited with being the first to combine the Habanera rhythm with a backbeat, a foundational element of their distinctive sound. "Dave Bartholomew and the musicians who worked with him, were the first ones to put together."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 8: The Fat Man and Fats Domino

podcast.title: Matassa and Bartholomew - Quintessential New Orleans Sound
podcast.body: The collaborations between Cosimo Matassa as engineer and Dave Bartholomew with his band produced quintessential New Orleans records that, even after 70 years, remain definitive of the city's unique sound. "the records that Matassa would go onto engineer with Dave Bartholomew in his band... would be the quintessential New Orleans records that still, 70 years on, sum up the sound of that city."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 8: The Fat Man and Fats Domino

podcast.title: Producer and Co-Writer for Fats Domino
podcast.body: Dave Bartholomew served as a producer and co-writer for Fats Domino, contributing original compositions to Domino's singles. He also brought "Treceo rhythms," described as having a "jelly roll, molten, Spanish tinge," to his arrangements, which became a signature element of New Orleans R&B. "One side of each of his singles would be written by Domino or his producer Dave Bartholomew."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Signature Bass Line Motif
podcast.body: Dave Bartholomew frequently incorporated a distinctive bass line motif into his arrangements, which became a staple of New Orleans R&B. He used this bass line in "Ain't That a Shame" and also in "Blue Monday," a song he wrote for Smiley Lewis. "It seems to have been taken up by Bartholomew as a signature motif."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Treheo Rhythm - Connection from Gottschalk to Bartholomew
podcast.body: The distinctive horn part in "Country Boy" is linked to Louis Moreau Gottschalk's compositions through its incorporation of the Treheo rhythm. "we can link that horn part back to the gut-shock piece we heard earlier, by its use of a rhythm called the Treheo."
